learningObjectives: Demonstrate how to validate the CSS properties of an element during tests in Testim.
Explain the method to validate data-driven actions such as clicking login, displaying login text, generating an email, and setting a password while testing an application.
Perform custom validations for actions not included in the predefined steps menu, such as extracting a user-defined value using custom scripts.
Verify whether a test case validation was successful based on custom validation steps.

elements.description: Checks any CSS property of an element. Property name takes a valid CSS property for the selected element (e.g. color, display, font-weight); Expected value is what that property should equal. The expected value can be a hardcoded literal (wrapped in quotes, e.g. 'red') or a parameter (entered by name, without quotes) — the same pattern used across other validation types.

The property name and/or expected value can be changed later without re-selecting the element. If the element itself needs to change, hover the target element thumbnail and click Reassign, then click the new element in the AUT window — the same Reassign mechanism used on any other step.

bulletPoints: Validate CSS property: Property name (a real CSS property) + Expected value (quoted literal or unquoted parameter name).
Changing just the expected property/value doesn't require reselecting the element; changing the element itself uses Reassign.

elements.term: Data-driven validation in a real flow
elements.description: Independent signup example: assert the required heading and resulting registered account using supported text/visibility/custom checks. Add intermediate assertions where they establish meaningful requirements or help diagnosis; asserting every typed value is not a universal Testim requirement. Generating a string does not create a working email inbox or prove a password was accepted.

elements.text: This ties together earlier modules directly: Generate random value/date for the dynamic data, Validate element text/visible for the resulting UI state, and Parameters to carry the generated value between steps.

bulletPoints: Choose meaningful intermediate and final assertions for the required behavior.
This is where Generate random value/date, Parameters, and Validate element text/visible come together in one flow.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Custom validations for actions beyond the predefined menu

elements.description: Browser custom steps can inspect DOM/HTML parameters. Node.js CLI steps are a separate execution path with their own runtime and supported package setup; local execution requires the connected Testim CLI and documented entitlement.

For a synchronous browser custom validation, return an explicit boolean. False or a thrown error can fail the check; timeout and failure handling also matter. Supported asynchronous examples return a Promise that resolves/rejects. The final synchronous true/false value is not the entire contract for every custom or CLI step.

elements.term: Extracting a user-defined value for custom checks
elements.description: Extract selected AUT text into a variable and reference it in a supported later validation or custom-code scope. Numeric/date matches can remain strings and require deliberate conversion; not every field accepts parameter references.

bulletPoints: Browser custom validation and Node.js CLI steps use different runtimes.
Synchronous boolean checks and asynchronous returned Promises have different completion contracts.
Reference extracted values only in supported scope/fields.

elements.description: After a run, a passed validation step shows its icon (upper-left corner of the step) in green, with a confirming message in the Properties panel. A failed validation step shows that same icon in red, with a failure message in the Properties panel — the same visual pattern applies to custom validation steps as to any predefined validation.

bulletPoints: Passed step = green icon (upper-left) + success message in Properties.
Failed step = red icon (upper-left) + failure message in Properties — same pattern for custom and predefined validations alike.

examPitfalls.title: Forgetting Validate CSS property's expected value needs quotes for literals
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Typing a literal expected value without quotes, which Testim then tries to interpret as a parameter name instead of a literal string.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Wrap a hardcoded literal in quotes (e.g. 'red'). Leave a parameter name unquoted — that distinction is how Testim tells the two apart.

examPitfalls.title: Returning something other than a clean boolean from a custom validation
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Writing a custom validation that returns a truthy/falsy non-boolean value, or forgets to return at all, producing an ambiguous pass/fail result.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Return an explicit boolean for a synchronous browser check. For asynchronous checks, return the supported Promise and validate rejection/timeout behavior; do not let unfinished work escape completion tracking.

examPitfalls.title: Only validating the final outcome of a multi-step data-driven flow
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Checking only that a signup completed successfully, without validating the intermediate generated email, the login text, or the password field along the way.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Assert meaningful requirements and final outcomes. Intermediate checks can improve evidence, but neither every input check nor one successful visual assertion guarantees full business coverage.

practiceQuiz.scenario: In a Validate CSS property step, how do you supply a hardcoded expected value versus a parameter?

options.text: Hardcoded values are wrapped in quotes; parameter names are entered without quotes.
Hardcoded values are entered without quotes; parameter names are wrapped in quotes.
Both must always be wrapped in quotes.
Parameters cannot be used in a Validate CSS property step.

practiceQuiz.hint: Quotes signal a literal string; no quotes signals a reference.
practiceQuiz.rationale: In the Expected value field, a hardcoded value is placed between quotes (e.g. 'red'), while a parameter value is entered by name without quotes — that distinction is how Testim tells a literal apart from a reference.

optionExplanations.A: The documented expected-value syntax distinguishes quoted literals and parameter references.
optionExplanations.B: This reverses literal and reference syntax.
optionExplanations.C: Quoting a parameter name makes it a string, not the reference.
optionExplanations.D: Parameter references are supported in the expected-value field.

practiceQuiz.scenario: For a completed synchronous browser custom validation with no thrown error, which explicit boolean result indicates success?

options.text: The string "pass".
A boolean true.
The number 1.
Nothing — it always passes unless it throws an error.

practiceQuiz.hint: The question is scoped to a synchronous browser boolean check.
practiceQuiz.rationale: True is the documented synchronous success result. False, exceptions and timeouts can indicate failure; asynchronous returned-Promise handling is a separate supported pattern.

optionExplanations.A: The question asks for an explicit boolean result, not a string.
optionExplanations.B: True is the documented synchronous boolean success result.
optionExplanations.C: Use the explicit boolean rather than relying on numeric truthiness.
optionExplanations.D: A missing return is not the documented boolean success contract.

practiceQuiz.scenario: How can a value be captured from the application and reused inside a later custom validation's logic?

options.text: It cannot be reused — custom validations can only use hardcoded values.
Using the Extract Value step to capture it into a parameter, then referencing that parameter later.
By manually retyping the value into every step that needs it.
Only by editing the project's base URL.

practiceQuiz.hint: It's the same Extract Value mechanism covered earlier in the path.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The Extract Value step captures a value from the app into a new parameter, which can then be used in a validation (including a custom validation's own code), a Set Text step, or other later steps — not something requiring manual retyping or unsupported.

optionExplanations.A: Supported parameter references can be used by later custom checks.
optionExplanations.B: Extract Value captures selected text into a reusable variable with appropriate scope.
optionExplanations.C: Manual retyping is not required for parameter reuse.
optionExplanations.D: Changing the base URL does not capture the required application value.

practiceQuiz.scenario: After a test run, how can you tell whether a specific validation step passed or failed?

options.text: There is no per-step indicator — only the overall test result matters.
The step's icon (upper-left) turns green with a success message, or red with a failure message, in the Properties panel.
Passed steps disappear from the test entirely.
Only custom validations show a status; predefined validations show nothing.

practiceQuiz.hint: It's a consistent green/red pattern, for both predefined and custom validations.
practiceQuiz.rationale: A passed validation shows a green icon in the step's upper-left corner with a confirming message in Properties; a failed one shows red with a failure message — the same pattern applies whether it's a predefined validation or a custom one.

optionExplanations.A: Executed validation steps have status and result messages.
optionExplanations.B: The documented result uses the step icon plus Properties messages.
optionExplanations.C: Passed steps are not removed from the definition.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A signup test must establish the heading and registered-account outcome. Which assertion approach covers those requirements without treating every typed value as a universal rule?

options.text: Only validate that the final signup confirmation appears, ignoring the intermediate steps.
Assert the required heading and registered-account outcome, adding relevant intermediate checks for requirements and diagnosis.
Skip validations entirely since the data is randomly generated.
Use only a single Visual Validation step for the whole flow.

practiceQuiz.hint: Validate required behavior rather than every input by default.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Meaningful intermediate and final assertions provide evidence for the stated requirements. Random inputs or a single visual check do not establish all required outcomes; no assertion strategy guarantees exact root-cause localization.

optionExplanations.A: The required heading check would be omitted.
optionExplanations.B: These assertions establish the stated heading and account requirements.
optionExplanations.C: Random inputs do not remove the need for assertions.
optionExplanations.D: One visual check does not establish all required functional outcomes.

quickRecap.value: Property name + Expected value; quoted = literal, unquoted = parameter.
Reassign via the target element thumbnail — same as any other step.
Assert meaningful requirements and final outcomes; intermediate checks are scenario-specific.
Synchronous browser checks return booleans; supported asynchronous checks return Promises. Exceptions/timeouts also matter.
Captures a value into a parameter, reusable in later validations and custom code.
Green step icon + Properties message = pass; red + failure message = fail.
